items.title: Sodium burns to make table salt — and then keeps wanting to react
items.claim: Sodium chloride formation looks like the textbook ionic reaction. Yet ionising Na to Na+ (+496 kJ/mol) and adding electron to Cl (-349 kJ/mol) gives a net cost of +147 kJ/mol. Why does it happen at all?
items.prompt: Where does the energy come from?

options.text: From the heat of the burning reaction
The lattice enthalpy — the enormous release of energy when Na+ and Cl- assemble into the crystal (around minus 787 kJ/mol) — dwarfs the cost of making the ions
From nowhere — the reaction is technically not spontaneous

items.reveal:
The full Born-Haber cycle for NaCl: atomise Na (+107), atomise Cl (+122), ionise Na (+496), add electron to Cl (-349), assemble lattice (-787). Net: -411 kJ/mol — exothermic and spontaneous.

Ionic bonding is NOT 'Na giving an electron to Cl' as the simple GCSE diagram suggests. It's the electrostatic stabilisation of a 3D crystal lattice. Lose the lattice (e.g., dissolve in water), and the bond is gone. NaCl(s) is stable; isolated NaCl molecules barely exist outside the gas phase.
items.why: The dot-and-cross diagram hides the energetics. Lattice enthalpy is where ionic compounds get their stability.

items.title: Water has the highest specific heat of any common liquid
items.claim: It takes 4.18 J to warm 1 g of water by 1°C. The same amount of energy raises 1 g of iron by 9.3°C, 1 g of copper by 11°C, 1 g of mercury by 30°C. Water is exceptionally hard to warm — and to cool.
items.prompt: Why is water's heat capacity so high?

options.text: Heat energy in water is shared between molecular vibrations, rotations, and the breaking and re-forming of hydrogen bonds; the hydrogen-bonding 'sink' absorbs huge amounts of energy with only modest temperature rise
Water is denser than most liquids

items.reveal:
When you heat water, energy doesn't just speed molecules up. A significant fraction goes into stretching and breaking hydrogen bonds. These bonds are about 23 kJ/mol — much smaller than O-H covalent bonds (463 kJ/mol) but much larger than typical thermal energy.

This is why coastal climates are mild: oceans absorb and release heat slowly. The Gulf Stream warms northwest Europe by carrying tropical heat north. Water's heat capacity buffers the climate.

It's also why sweating cools you so effectively: evaporating 1 g of water absorbs 2260 J (latent heat of vaporisation) — far more than the same mass of any common solvent.
items.why: Specific heat is taught as a number to look up. It is a measure of how many ways a substance can absorb energy at the molecular level.

items.title: Rust costs the world about 3 percent of global GDP every year
items.claim: The NACE International IMPACT study (2016) estimated the global cost of corrosion at 2.5 trillion US dollars per year — about 3.4 percent of global GDP. Bridges, ships, pipelines, vehicles, buildings: the world fights iron's tendency to oxidise.
items.prompt: What makes iron-based rust particularly destructive?

options.text: Iron oxide (Fe2O3) has greater volume than the iron it formed from, so it flakes off rather than forming a protective layer; underlying metal is constantly exposed, and the process continues until the structure fails
Iron rusts in a chain reaction

items.reveal:
When aluminium oxidises, Al2O3 has nearly the same molar volume as the metal, forming a tight, protective coating. When iron oxidises, hydrated Fe2O3 occupies more space than the metal, breaks free, flakes off, and exposes fresh iron to the next round.

The Pilling-Bedworth ratio for iron is about 2.1 (oxide volume vs metal volume). For aluminium it's about 1.3. A ratio close to 1 gives a protective layer; ratios much larger than 1 give flaking; ratios much smaller than 1 give porous, useless layers.

Protection strategies: galvanising (zinc sacrificial anode), painting (barrier coating), stainless-steel alloying with Cr (which forms protective Cr2O3), cathodic protection (applied voltage), and design choices to keep moisture off.
items.why: Rust is taught as 'iron + oxygen + water'. The economics and the engineering of corrosion control are vast.
